title: Measuring and Generating Sequences with len and range
content:
What problem does this solve?
You need to know how many items are in a list, or repeat an action a fixed number of turns, or walk a list by index when the position matters.

Basic syntax
  len(party)
  for turn in range(3):
      print(turn)
  for i in range(len(items)):
      print(i, items[i])

What actually happens
len counts elements. range(n) produces 0, 1, …, n-1 — the stop value is never included. range(len(items)) gives valid index numbers for a list.

When this is useful
Use len for counts, range(n) for a known number of repetitions, and range(len(seq)) when you need both index and value.
concepts: len(sequence) returns how many items it holds
range(n) counts from 0 up to but not including n
range(len(items)) pairs each index with items[index]

examples.title: Three combat turns
examples.explanation: range(3) yields 0, 1, 2 — add 1 when displaying to humans.

examples.title: Number inventory slots by index
examples.explanation: i is 0 then 1; adding 1 makes human-friendly line numbers.

common_mistakes: Treating range(3) as 1, 2, 3 — it starts at 0 and stops before 3
Using items[len(items)] — the last valid index is len(items) - 1
Forgetting that an empty list has len 0 and no valid index

exercises.title: Predict the last value
exercises.prompt: range(3) prints several numbers. What is the last value printed? Trace the loop, then click Check.
exercises.failure_message: range(3) produces 0, 1, then 2 — the last value printed is 2, not 3.
hints: range(3) stops before 3, so the values are 0, 1, 2.
Each loop prints one value; track the final i.

exercises.title: Loop the right number of turns
exercises.prompt: Print Turn 1, Turn 2, and Turn 3 using range. Replace None with the correct range call.
exercises.starter_code:
for turn in None:  # TODO: three turns, indexes 0..2
    print(f"Turn {turn + 1}")
hints: range with one argument stops before that number.
Use range(3) to get indexes 0, 1, and 2.

tests.message: Use a for loop over range.

exercises.title: Fix the off-by-one index
exercises.prompt:
This program should print the last inventory item (potion) without crashing. It uses an index one past the end.

Run to see the error, fix the index, then Check.
hints: Run first — valid indexes go from 0 through len(items) - 1.
The last item sits at index len(items) - 1.

tests.name: items
tests.message: Read from items using a valid index.

exercises.title: Return the last item
exercises.prompt:
Write last_item(items) that returns the last element of a non-empty list.

If items is empty, return None. Do not print.
hints: The last index is len(items) - 1, or use items[-1].
Return None for an empty list; otherwise return the last element.

tests.message: The last of three items should be potion.
A one-item list should return that item.
An empty list should return None, not crash.
Use indexing that works for any length, not a hardcoded answer.

exercises.title: Numbered inventory lines
exercises.prompt:
Write numbered_lines(items) that returns a list of strings like:
["1. sword", "2. shield"]

Use range(len(items)) to build each line. Return the list — do not print.
exercises.starter_code:
def numbered_lines(items):
    lines = []
    # Loop i over range(len(items)); append f"{i + 1}. {items[i]}"
    return lines
exercises.success_message: You combined len, range, indexing, and f-strings to label every item — a pattern party rosters will reuse later.
hints: Start with an empty list to collect lines.
Each line is an f-string: number is i + 1, text is items[i].
Append each line, then return the full list.

tests.message: Two items should produce two numbered lines.
A single item should be line 1.
Line text must come from the items, not hardcoded sword/shield.
An empty inventory should return an empty list.
Line numbers must increase by one each time.
